title: Frame a short wall section: set three studs on their layout marks and screw each through the bottom plate
instruction: Frame the wall section: stand each stud on edge between the plates on its layout marks, then drive the screw at its mark through the bottom plate into the stud's end with an impact driver until the head is flush.
context: Carpenters (O*NET 47-2031.00, 0.7 million in the US) frame walls flat on the deck or a framing table ('Assemble and fasten materials to make framework'). The plates are marked at every stud, 16 in on centre, and the fasteners are started at each mark, as hand framers start their nails; each stud is set on edge on its marks and fastened through the plate into its end with framing nails or structural framing screws. A stud off its mark throws off the sheathing joints on it, and a loose stud is pulled and reset. The task needs precise control of position: each stud goes into a gap only 6 mm longer than itself, onto marks within 4 mm, and the impact driver's bit must be pressed into the screw's head, on its axis, with at least 20 N, trigger squeezed, and kept there as the screw goes 38 mm in, drawing the stud tight; if the bit slips out, the stud stays loose. The top plate's screws, driven from the far side, out of the arms' reach, are not part of this task.
setup: Dream Labs' YAM station (scene=station), both arms starting at their ready pose. World frame: origin between the arm bases, x forward, y to the left, z up; the table top is at z = 0.7475 m. Framing table, fixed: a 3/4 in (19 mm) plywood board 40.7 cm (x 0.198 to 0.605 m) by 96.4 cm (y -0.482 to 0.482 m) flat on the table; on it two 2x4 plates (38 x 89 mm, spruce-pine-fir, 33.5 in = 85.1 cm long, centred at y 0) standing on edge across the table: the bottom plate on the arms' side (x 0.218 to 0.256 m) and the top plate on the far side (x 0.567 to 0.605 m), 31.1 cm apart, a stud's length plus 6 mm. Both plates carry pencil layout marks (two lines 38 mm apart on each plate's top edge) for three studs 16 in on centre, at y -0.406, 0 and 0.406 m; the end studs are flush with the plates' ends. At each mark, a pair of pine stops (3/4 x 1-1/2 x 6 in, 19 x 38 x 152 mm, their tops rounded over toward the gap with a 19 mm radius) stands against the top plate's face, 44.1 mm apart (3 mm each side of a stud). At each mark, a #10 x 3 in (4.8 x 76 mm) black-coated wood screw with a #2 square-drive head (9.8 mm across) sits in a 3/16 in clearance hole through the bottom plate, its tip flush with the plate's inner face and its head 38 mm proud, at z 0.811 m (the studs' mid-depth). Studs: three surfaced spruce-pine-fir 2x4s cut to 12 in (38 x 89 x 305 mm, 0.47 kg) standing on edge on the table, length along x, centres at x 0.30 m: one at y 0.585 m turned 3.4 degrees clockwise, and two at y -0.53 and -0.61 m turned 1.7 degrees counterclockwise and clockwise (seen from above). Two compact 12 V cordless impact drivers of the common 12 V class (such as Milwaukee M12 or Bosch 12V; 0.95 kg with a 2 Ah battery; 1/4 in hex chuck with a 1 in #2 square bit; the trigger on the grip's front, about 40 x 28 mm, at the grip's balance point), one for each hand, lying on their sides on low plastic rests in front of the table with their bits toward the plates and their grips toward the robot's left: the left one's bit tip at (0.21, 0.369) m, the right one's at (0.16, -0.071) m, 3.6 cm above the table. All objects share one rubber-like friction (static 1.2, dynamic 1.0). The layout is fixed (-E object_jitter=0). For a real trial, screw the plates and stops to the plywood and clamp the board to the table.
scoring: Each stud scores up to 1/3 on its own, and each mark credits at most one stud. Placed, 0.10: the stud stands on edge between the plates (its 89 mm face upright within 3 degrees), square to the plates within 3 degrees, its bottom within 3 mm of the plywood, and its centre line within 4 mm of the centre of its marks (tape measure across the marks). Caught, 0.10 more: its screw has gone into the stud's end (in a real trial, the stud can no longer be lifted out). Fastened, 0.133 more: the screw is driven home, its head within 1 mm of flush with the plate (a straightedge across the plate's face, or a 1 mm feeler gauge that will not go under the head's edge), and the stud's end is tight to the bottom plate (a 1 mm feeler gauge does not go into the joint). A screw driven with no stud on its marks catches nothing; a stud anywhere else (lying flat, on the stops' tops, off its marks, tilted, turned or on the table) scores 0. Score = the sum, at the end of the trial; the trial ends as a success once all three studs are fastened with both hands at least 3 cm from every stud, held for 1 s.
reset_notes: In simulation nothing is consumed. Real trials: back each screw out until its tip is flush with the bottom plate's inner face again and stand the studs back at their starting places; turn a stud end for end, or swap in a fresh one cut to 12 in, once the screw hole in its end is worn (about every ten trials). Set the drivers to their lowest speed mode and keep people clear of the arms while they run.
fidelity: Lumber, plywood, stops and screws are boxes and cylinders at real sizes; each driver is boxes and cylinders, 0.95 kg, its trigger a block. Screws are our model, not PhysX threads: a screw turns in only while PhysX reports the driver's bit touching its head and pressing it with at least 20 N, and a pad pressing the trigger with at least 17 N; its thread catches the stud at the plate and draws it tight. The stops' rounded tops are spheres. One screw per stud end. Friction 1.2/1.0.
